newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers urge Fed not to raise interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers urge Fed not to raise interest rates.

text.p: A group of lawmakers urged the Federal Reserve Friday not to raise interest rates at its policy-making meeting next month, saying it would threaten economic growth.

"The Federal Reserve shouldn't further raise interest rates," House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri said. "Our people and our businesses can't afford it. And our economy hasn't overheated so much that the Fed needs to apply the brakes."
The Fed needs to adopt a new approach, Gephardt said. "They need to help promote growth and a rising standard of living rather than view prosperity as a threat to our economy," he said.
The lawmakers sent a letter to Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan that said "now is not the time to further raise interest rates and put economic growth and opportunity at risk."
The letter was signed by 62 Democrats, one Republican, Representative Jim Bunning of Kentucky, and one independent, Representative Bernard Sanders of Vermont.
The Fed raised short-term interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point March 25. The next meeting of the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee is May 20.
Sen. Tom Harkin, an Iowa Democrat, said he was going to take a "long, hard look" at President Clinton's nominees to two vacancies on the Fed Board.
Harkin, who has long been a critic of the Fed, helped hold up Greenspan's renomination to another term as Fed chairman last year. Greenspan was eventually confirmed.
Clinton plans to name Roger Ferguson, a partner with consulting firm McKinsey & Co. Inc., and Edward Gramlich, a University of Michigan economist, to fill the vacancies.
Harkin said he has instructed his staff to obtain economic writings by the two expected nominees.
"The early indications are we're going to have more of the same from these two nominees," Harkin said. "I don't want to prejudge them, but ... early indications are they're just cookie cutters."
"I'm not about to rubber-stamp anybody," Harkin said. He added he would seek to have extensive debate on the Senate floor on the two Fed nominees, "maybe even more so than on Mr. Greenspan."
Harkin's demand for floor time on Greenspan's nomination last year held up that nomination for weeks.
